record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text and portions of the extracted text are garbled, but the main text and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It measures neuron-level selectivity across linguistic contrasts with a new minimal-pair metric, and directly tests how selectivity classifications vary with thresholds and scoring metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper reports raw separability and NSI results, threshold sweeps, alternative similarity metrics, pairing and deletion controls, cross-checkpoint summaries, and ablations. Results cited from other work are not recorded. The paper's probe-versus-behavior comparisons are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper names polysemanticity as motivation and calls tuning breadth a polysemanticity proxy. Its results bear on a different construct: how selectively last-token residual-stream dimensions separate grammatical from ungrammatical minimal pairs in related linguistic paradigms. No result counts units responding to unrelated inputs, and none is from MLP neurons. The threshold and metric sweeps change how many units count as selective for one paradigm, not whether a unit counts as polysemantic. Breadth, the polysemanticity proxy, is reported only at NSI>0, so its dependence on measurement is not tested. These findings go under fits_no_version rather than V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Missing points: raw separability peaks earlier for morphology and syntax than for conceptual contrasts. Whole-vector probe accuracy is essentially uncorrelated with behaviour (r = −0.032). Selectivity, decodability and behavioural reliance are presented as dissociated. The ablation 'units' are residual-stream dimensions, and the authors say the null does not prove they are irrelevant.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses last-token activations, matched linguistic minimal pairs, Pearson-correlation separability, and a permutation-normalized NSI; it is not a reproduction of the cited vision-neuron or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The classification counts depend strongly on the NSI threshold. Spearman and cosine produce different percentages above z > 2 than Pearson. Pair alignment changes the results: cross-item good–bad pairs produce many high-NSI outliers, while random same-label pairs produce none. Critical-token deletion nearly eliminates raw separability in the clean one-prefix subset. The main analysis uses 500 permutations; pairing controls use 200.

fits_no_version.finding: For Qwen3-0.6B residual-stream dimensions, the share of units counted as selective for a grammatical paradigm falls from 3.70% at NSI>0 to 0.094% at NSI>1 and 1.54e-4% at NSI≥1.645–3. Spearman and cosine variants give 0.222% and 0.277% above z>2. Pairing and deletion controls show raw separability depends on item matching.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether a unit counts as selective for a linguistic contrast depends strongly on the selectivity threshold and similarity metric, though strong selectivity stays rare under all variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Across seven checkpoints, 2.5–3.9% of units have positive NSI per paradigm. Mean breadth is 1.72–2.68 of 68 paradigms, and only 3 of 68 paradigms in Qwen3-0.6B have any NSI>2 unit. Even units responsive to ≥3 phenomena keep a dominant within-domain preference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-stream units in LLMs show sparse, weak and narrowly tuned selectivity for grammatical minimal-pair contrasts, with little broad cross-paradigm tuning.

record.problems: The study uses templated English BLiMP and COMPS minimal pairs and last-token residual-stream dimensions, which the authors say may miss information at earlier positions or in other components. The ablation test covers three paradigms in one checkpoint and reuses the same 1,000 minimal pairs for selection and evaluation. Empirical-null calibration is limited: no unit survives the reported Benjamini–Hochberg correction, and the authors note that the 200-permutation empirical p-values are too coarse for a powerful correction over 28,672 units. The study does not directly test unrelated tokens or contexts in MLP neurons.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every layer-wise curve, paradigm-level distribution, or ablation condition; those results do not test V7's stated measurement-dependence claim as directly as the threshold, metric, pairing, and deletion results retained. Ablation and probe-versus-behavior results are not rows for the tested version.

untested.parts: No vision models or image inputs.

Analyses last-token residual-stream dimensions, not MLP neurons. Tests related grammatical/conceptual contrasts rather than responses to unrelated tokens or contexts. No share of polysemantic neurons is reported.
Superposition is mentioned only as a possible explanation for the null ablation result; it is not tested.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not examined.
Seven checkpoints are compared, but activation function and regularization are not varied. No polysemanticity rate or performance trade-off is reported.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined. The poly-selective neurons' dominant within-domain preference (Figure 6) concerns related grammatical phenomena, not unrelated mixtures.
Breadth (the polysemanticity proxy) is reported only at NSI>0. Neither activation range nor explanation scoring is varied for polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 'supports' label is removed. The threshold and metric sweeps concern counts of paradigm-selective units, not polysemanticity. Units are scalar dimensions of the last-token residual stream ('each scalar dimension as a neuron'), not MLP neurons. Superposition and polysemanticity appear only in the introduction and as one possible explanation for the null ablation results.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns language models and linguistic contrasts, not vision models or image inputs.
It analyzes last-token residual-stream dimensions, not specifically MLP neurons, and tests grammatical and conceptual minimal-pair paradigms rather than unrelated tokens or contexts.
Superposition or capacity pressure is not manipulated or tested as a cause of selectivity.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise are not tested as causes.
The paper compares checkpoints from model families but does not test activation-function changes, modern convolutional architectures, or performance costs of reducing polysemanticity.
It does not investigate whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect a shared feature such as pose, or establish that unrelated mixtures are rare under better feature explanations.
It varies selectivity thresholds and similarity metrics, and examines pairing controls; it does not vary which activation range or token position is examined.
